name: Treaty with the Potawatomi, 1828 (Treaty of Carey Mission)
aka: Treaty at the Missionary Establishments upon the St. Joseph, 1828
promises: Article 2: an additional permanent annuity of $2,000 and an additional annuity of $1,000 for twenty years; $30,000 in goods at or soon after signing; $10,000 in goods and $5,000 in specie in 1829.

Article 2: $7,500 to be spent for the tribe on clearing and fencing land, houses, domestic animals, farm tools and labourers; 2,000 pounds of tobacco, 1,500 weight of iron and 350 pounds of steel each year.

Article 2: $1,000 a year for education for as long as Congress thought it useful; the blacksmith promised by the treaty of Chicago for fifteen years to be supported permanently; three labourers four months a year for ten years for the band on the reservation south of the St. Joseph.
Article 3: land grants to the persons named, to be located on the second cession, not conveyable without the President's consent.
Article 4: $10,895 to be applied to claims against the tribe listed in an annexed schedule.

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found that the consideration the United States paid the Potawatomi under four treaties, this one among them (Royce areas 145 and 146), came to $922,525.00 for interests in land with a combined fair market value of $5,420,340.59, and was so grossly inadequate as to be unconscionable. The Commission did not state a separate figure for this treaty.

landTaken: Royce area 145 (Michigan), from the mouth of the St. Joseph of Lake Michigan to the Indiana line, and area 146 (Indiana), south of the 1817 line east of the southern end of Lake Michigan (Article 1). The Commission found the Potawatomi held recognized title to area 145, to the part of area 146 north of the Wabash watershed and to a one-half interest in the rest of area 146, with the Miami holding the other half; the valuation date was January 7, 1829.
compensation: The Article 2 annuities, goods, specie, services and supplies. The Commission set the Potawatomi consideration under the four treaties at $922,525.00 in all and awarded $4,497,815.59 for the four treaties together on September 8, 1978, subject to offsets.
today: The 1978 award covers four treaties without a separate figure for this one. On September 29, 1978 the Commission certified Dockets 128 et al. to the United States Court of Claims; the final judgment and payment were not traced in this pass.

plain.promised: A further permanent annuity of $2,000 and $1,000 a year for twenty years, $30,000 in goods at signing, money for farms, houses and schooling, a permanent blacksmith, and yearly tobacco, iron and steel.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1978 that the $922,525.00 paid under four treaties, this one among them, for land worth $5,420,340.59 was so grossly inadequate as to be unconscionable.
plain.today: In 1978 the Commission awarded $4,497,815.59 for the four treaties together, subject to offsets, with no separate figure for this one. The final judgment and whether it was paid have not been traced.

nationVoice.summary: The Band's history says the Potawatomi lived in what is now Wisconsin, southern Michigan, northern Indiana and northern Illinois, that as the frontier moved west boundary arguments and land cessions became a way of life, and that the 1833 Treaty of Chicago then set the terms for removing the Potawatomi from the Great Lakes.
The Community's cultural preservation pages publish the full text of the treaty of 20 September 1828, with its schedule of traders' claims, without further commentary.

openQuestions: treaties.json has no Kappler link for this entry; the treaty is in Kappler vol. 2 at p. 294 (Oklahoma State University page treaty-with-the-potawatomi-1828-0294).
The per-treaty value and consideration in the Commission's 1978 tables did not come through in the scanned text; only the four-treaty totals are recorded.
The Court of Claims judgment after the 1978 transfer, and whether the award was paid, were not traced.
Whether the permanent blacksmith, the education money and the labourers were provided was not researched.
No Potawatomi nation's own account of this treaty was found in this pass. To-pen-e-bee and Po-ka-gon are among the signers; the Pokagon Band's history is the first place to look.

Audit 2026-11-08: the September 29, 1978 certification to the Court of Claims in 'today' had no source; the Commission's order of that date (43 Ind. Cl. Comm. 675) was opened and added to sources. Figures, dates and the treaty text were checked and stand.
